hints.content: Point at each shape in turn and name it out loud: this one, this one, this one. Do not ask for an answer yet.
Read the question again and put your finger on the word that says which way to look: biggest or smallest, more or fewer.
Ask about one shape at a time. Comparing three at once is more than a three-year-old can hold.
Cover the shape they chose with your hand and ask the question again about the two that are left.
Bring in something real: two cups, two spoons, two piles of blocks. Ask the same question about those first.
Put your finger on each shape and say the question again for that one alone: is this the one?
Say what the question is really asking about: how much space it covers. Then ask it about each shape separately.
If the answer keeps changing, the child is guessing rather than looking. Slow down and go back to two shapes.
Their rule is probably picking the middle one, or picking the opposite of what was asked. Show a pair where that rule gives the wrong answer, and let them see it fail.
Act it out away from the screen. Compare two of the same thing in the room, then come back to the picture.
Work one all the way through out loud yourself, saying why each shape is or is not the answer.
Name how much space it covers first, check it on every shape, and only then choose. Expect this to take several tries over several days.

Touch each thing in the question picture and count out loud together: one, two, three. Do not ask for an answer yet.
Count the question picture again out loud, then say that last number once more. That is the number being looked for.
Take one group at a time. Holding three of them in mind at once is more than a three-year-old can do.
Cover the group they chose with your hand and count the question picture again together, slowly.
Use real things. Put out that many buttons or blocks, then look for the group on screen that has the same.
Put a finger on each thing as you say each number. One number, one thing, every time.
What the question asks about is how many things are in it, and nothing else about the picture. Count each group on its own and say each total out loud.
If the count comes out differently each time, the fingers and the words are out of step. Go back to three things and slow the counting right down.
Their rule is probably picking the group with the biggest things in it, or the one spread out widest. Show a pair where that rule gives the wrong answer, and let them see it fail.
